claim: The rodent olfactory bulb incorporates thousands of newly generated inhibitory neurons daily throughout adulthood.
source: The rodent olfactory bulb incorporates thousands of newly generated inhibitory neurons daily throughout adulthood, but the role of adult neurogenesis in olfactory processing is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by general scientific knowledge about adult neurogenesis in the olfactory bulb.

claim: Mice without young adult-born neurons showed normal ability in discriminating very different odorants.
source: Mice without young adult-born neurons (ABNs) showed normal ability in discriminating very different odorants but were impaired in fine discrimination.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2C showing no significant difference between control and ablation groups in easy discrimination task.

claim: Mice without young adult-born neurons were impaired in fine discrimination.
source: Mice without young adult-born neurons (ABNs) showed normal ability in discriminating very different odorants but were impaired in fine discrimination.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E showing significantly lower performance in ablation animals during difficult discrimination task (p(group)<0.0001).

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging of mitral cells revealed that ensemble odor representations of similar odorants were more ambiguous in ablation animals.
source: Furthermore, two-photon calcium imaging of mitral cells (MCs) revealed that the ensemble odor representations of similar odorants were more ambiguous in the ablation animals.
evidence: Supported by decoder analysis data in Figure 4E showing lower decoder accuracy in ablation animals (p(group)<0.05).

claim: The increased ambiguity in odor representations was primarily due to a decrease in MC suppressive responses.
source: This increased ambiguity was primarily due to a decrease in MC suppressive responses.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5C showing significantly reduced suppressive responses in ablation animals (p<0.0001).

claim: Deficits in MC encoding were only observed during task engagement but not passive exposure.
source: Intriguingly, these deficits in MC encoding were only observed during task engagement but not passive exposure.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7A-C showing no significant differences between control and ablation during passive exposure.

claim: Young olfactory ABNs are essential for the enhancement of MC pattern separation in a task engagement-dependent manner.
source: Our results indicate that young olfactory ABNs are essential for the enhancement of MC pattern separation in a task engagement-dependent manner, potentially functioning as a gateway for top-down modulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined behavioral and imaging data showing task-dependent effects of ABN ablation.

claim: Young olfactory ABNs potentially function as a gateway for top-down modulation.
source: Our results indicate that young olfactory ABNs are essential for the enhancement of MC pattern separation in a task engagement-dependent manner, potentially functioning as a gateway for top-down modulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the task-dependent effects and known centrifugal inputs to ABNs.

claim: The subventricular zone (SVZ) is one of the two main loci in the rodent brain where adult neurogenesis takes place.
source: The subventricular zone (SVZ) is one of the two main loci in the rodent brain where adult neurogenesis takes place (Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2008.

claim: New neurons produced in the SVZ migrate through the rostral migratory stream to the olfactory bulb.
source: In the SVZ, many thousands of new neurons are produced each day throughout adulthood, and these new neurons migrate through the rostral migratory stream to the olfactory bulb (Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994), the first olfactory center of the brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994.

claim: About 95% of adult-born neurons differentiate into granule cells.
source: Once in the olfactory bulb, about 95% of the adult-born neurons (ABNs) differentiate into granule cells (GCs) and the majority of the remaining differentiate into periglomerular cells (Lledo et al., 2006), both of which are GABAergic local inhibitory neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lledo et al., 2006.

claim: The majority of the remaining adult-born neurons differentiate into periglomerular cells.
source: Once in the olfactory bulb, about 95% of the adult-born neurons (ABNs) differentiate into granule cells (GCs) and the majority of the remaining differentiate into periglomerular cells (Lledo et al., 2006), both of which are GABAergic local inhibitory neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lledo et al., 2006.

claim: Both granule cells and periglomerular cells are GABAergic local inhibitory neurons.
source: Once in the olfactory bulb, about 95% of the adult-born neurons (ABNs) differentiate into granule cells (GCs) and the majority of the remaining differentiate into periglomerular cells (Lledo et al., 2006), both of which are GABAergic local inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neurotransmitter phenotype of these cell types.

claim: Granule cells inhibit mitral cells through dendrodendritic reciprocal connections.
source: GCs inhibit mitral cells (MCs), the principal neurons of the olfactory bulb, through their dendrodendritic reciprocal connections (Isaacson and Strowbridge, 1998; Rall et al., 1966; Shepherd, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citations to Isaacson and Strowbridge, 1998; Rall et al., 1966; Shepherd, 1963.

claim: Inhibition of MCs can sparsen odor representations and enhance the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: This inhibition of MCs can sparsen odor representations and enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (Koulakov and Rinberg, 2011; Yokoi et al., 1995; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koulakov and Rinberg, 2011; Yokoi et al., 1995; Yu et al., 2014.

claim: General activation of bulbar inhibitory neurons can accelerate learning.
source: Consistent with this idea, general activation of bulbar inhibitory neurons can accelerate learning (Abraham et al., 2010), while suppression of inhibitory neuron activity can increase the excitability of MCs and reduce MC pattern separation (Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abraham et al., 2010.

claim: Suppression of inhibitory neuron activity can increase the excitability of MCs and reduce MC pattern separation.
source: Consistent with this idea, general activation of bulbar inhibitory neurons can accelerate learning (Abraham et al., 2010), while suppression of inhibitory neuron activity can increase the excitability of MCs and reduce MC pattern separation (Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gschwend et al., 2015.

claim: ABNs display higher levels of morphological and functional plasticity during the first ~8 weeks after their birth compared to their later mature stage.
source: As ABNs integrate into local circuits, they display higher levels of morphological and functional plasticity during the first ~8 weeks after their birth compared to their later mature stage (Kelsch et al., 2009; Mizrahi, 2007; Nissant et al., 2009; Sailor et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kelsch et al., 2009; Mizrahi, 2007; Nissant et al., 2009; Sailor et al., 2016.

claim: The spine dynamics, synaptic plasticity, sensory response pattern, and survival rate of ABNs are influenced by olfactory experience during the early period.
source: Furthermore, the spine dynamics, synaptic plasticity, sensory response pattern, as well as survival rate of ABNs are influenced by olfactory experience during this early period (Alonso et al., 2006; Lemasson et al., 2005; Lepousez et al., 2014; Livneh et al., 2014; Mouret et al., 2008; Petreanu and Alvarez-Buylla, 2002; Quast et al., 2017; Rochefort et al., 2002; Yamaguchi and Mori, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing experience-dependent plasticity of ABNs.

claim: Some studies have shown that ABNs are essential for certain olfactory behaviors such as odor discrimination and association reversal learning.
source: Indeed, some studies have shown that ABNs are essential for certain olfactory behaviors such as odor discrimination and association reversal learning (Alonso et al., 2012; Bath et al., 2008; Enwere et al., 2004; Gheusi et al., 2000; Moreno et al., 2009; Sakamoto et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Other studies have found little effects of ABN manipulation on odor discrimination.
source: However, other studies have found little effects of ABN manipulation on odor discrimination (Breton-Provencher et al., 2009; Imayoshi et al., 2008; Lazarini et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing minimal effects.

claim: ABNs are not essential for all olfactory processing.
source: Thus, ABNs are not essential for all olfactory processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inconsistent results in the literature.

claim: The impact of ABNs may depend on the behavioral context.
source: Instead, the inconsistencies between these results raise the possibility that the impact of ABNs may depend on the behavioral context.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain inconsistent findings in the literature.

claim: Local inhibitory neurons in the olfactory bulb including ABNs receive abundant glutamatergic centrifugal inputs from higher brain areas.
source: Consistent with the idea that the functions of ABNs are context-dependent, local inhibitory neurons in the olfactory bulb including ABNs receive abundant glutamatergic centrifugal inputs from higher brain areas such as anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and entorhinal cortex (Balu et al., 2007; Boyd et al., 2015, 2012; Chapuis et al., 2013; Kiselycznyk et al., 2006; Markopoulos et al., 2012; Nunez-Parra et al., 2013; Otazu et al., 2015; Rothermel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting centrifugal inputs.

claim: Inhibitory neurons express a variety of neuromodulator receptors.
source: Inhibitory neurons also express a variety of neuromodulator receptors, which provide additional avenues for top-down modulation (Castillo et al., 1999; Devore and Linster, 2012; Ma and Luo, 2012; Moreno et al., 2012; Rothermel et al., 2014; Shipley et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing neuromodulator receptor expression.

claim: Anesthesia inactivates feedback fibers and reduces GC activity while increasing MC activity.
source: Furthermore, anesthesia inactivates feedback fibers and reduces GC activity while increasing MC activity (Kato et al., 2012; Rothermel and Wachowiak, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kato et al., 2012; Rothermel and Wachowiak, 2014.

claim: Bulbar inhibitory neurons may function as a mediator of feedback regulation to shape MC odor encoding.
source: Thus, bulbar inhibitory neurons may function as a mediator of feedback regulation to shape MC odor encoding (Markopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Markopoulos et al., 2012.

claim: Cortical feedback can decorrelate MC odor representations.
source: Consistent with this notion, it has been reported that cortical feedback can decorrelate MC odor representations (Otazu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Otazu et al., 2015.

claim: Neuromodulatory projections can modulate MC activity.
source: Similarly, neuromodulatory projections can modulate MC activity (Rothermel and Wachowiak, 2014) and improve perceptual learning (Ma and Luo, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rothermel and Wachowiak, 2014; Ma and Luo, 2012.

claim: Neuromodulatory projections can improve perceptual learning.
source: Similarly, neuromodulatory projections can modulate MC activity (Rothermel and Wachowiak, 2014) and improve perceptual learning (Ma and Luo, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma and Luo, 2012.

claim: VGCC administration results in a near-complete ablation of ABNs in the olfactory bulbs of Gfap-tk+ mice.
source: The ablation of adult neurogenesis in the olfactory bulb was nearly complete, shown by post-hoc BrdU labeling (p<0.0001, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Gfap-tk+ vs. Gfap-tk-; Figure 1C) as well as immunostaining for Doublecortin, a marker for immature neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by BrdU and Doublecortin immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: There was no difference in the density of GFAP-positive astrocytes in VGCC-treated Gfap-tk+ and Gfap-tk- mice in the olfactory bulb.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in the density of GFAP-positive astrocytes in VGCC-treated Gfap-tk+ and Gfap-tk- mice in the olfactory bulb (p=0.9911, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1E) nor in the hippocampus dentate gyrus (p=0.1359, Wilcoxon rank sum test), consistent with a previous report (Snyder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by GFAP immunostaining data in Figure 1E and citation to Snyder et al., 2011.

claim: There was no difference in the density of GFAP-positive astrocytes in VGCC-treated Gfap-tk+ and Gfap-tk- mice in the hippocampus dentate gyrus.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in the density of GFAP-positive astrocytes in VGCC-treated Gfap-tk+ and Gfap-tk- mice in the olfactory bulb (p=0.9911, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1E) nor in the hippocampus dentate gyrus (p=0.1359, Wilcoxon rank sum test), consistent with a previous report (Snyder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by statistical test result and citation to Snyder et al., 2011.

claim: Regeneration of olfactory sensory neurons is intact in the Gfap-tk mouse line.
source: Another previous report also showed that regeneration of olfactory sensory neurons is intact in this mouse line (Cummings et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cummings et al., 2014.

claim: Ablation mice showed no obvious general health impairment.
source: Ablation mice showed no obvious general health impairment, and demonstrated mobility and anxiety levels comparable to control mice in an open field test (average speed: p=1.0000, center time fraction: p=0.7984, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by open field test data in Figure 1F.

claim: Ablation mice demonstrated mobility and anxiety levels comparable to control mice in an open field test.
source: Ablation mice showed no obvious general health impairment, and demonstrated mobility and anxiety levels comparable to control mice in an open field test (average speed: p=1.0000, center time fraction: p=0.7984, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by open field test data in Figure 1F showing no significant differences.

claim: Both ablation and control animals achieved expertise in the easy discrimination task in equivalent durations of training.
source: Both ablation and control animals achieved expertise in this task (defined as >80% success rate) in equivalent durations of training (number of sessions, control: 4.18 ± 0.21, ablation: 4.39 ± 0.25, mean ±S.E.M; p=0.4523, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2C showing no significant difference.

claim: Young ABNs are not required for the performance of the easy discrimination task.
source: Thus, we conclude that young ABNs are not required for the performance of this easy discrimination task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing equivalent performance in easy discrimination.

claim: Ablation animals showed slower learning in the difficult discrimination task compared to control animals.
source: Although the performance of control animals was initially at chance level, it consistently improved over 10 sessions to achieve a success rate of 0.760 ± 0.017 in session 10. In contrast, ablation animals showed slower learning (comparison of linear regression slopes in individual animals, p=0.0100, Wilcoxon rank sum test), and their performance was significantly lower than that of the control animals (p(group)<0.0001, p(session)<0.0001, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E showing significantly different learning curves.

claim: The performance of ablation animals was significantly lower than that of control animals in the difficult discrimination task.
source: Although the performance of control animals was initially at chance level, it consistently improved over 10 sessions to achieve a success rate of 0.760 ± 0.017 in session 10. In contrast, ablation animals showed slower learning (comparison of linear regression slopes in individual animals, p=0.0100, Wilcoxon rank sum test), and their performance was significantly lower than that of the control animals (p(group)<0.0001, p(session)<0.0001, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E with statistical significance.

claim: Both control and ablation groups had comparable fractions of answered trials.
source: The deficits observed in ablation animals were unlikely due to problems in motivation or licking ability, as both groups had the comparable fractions of answered trials (control vs. ablation, p(group) = 0.4101, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2F) and the comparable licking rates during reward consumption (control vs. ablation, p(group) = 0.1036, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2F showing no significant difference.

claim: Both control and ablation groups had comparable licking rates during reward consumption.
source: The deficits observed in ablation animals were unlikely due to problems in motivation or licking ability, as both groups had the comparable fractions of answered trials (control vs. ablation, p(group) = 0.4101, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2F) and the comparable licking rates during reward consumption (control vs. ablation, p(group) = 0.1036, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2G showing no significant difference.

claim: Mice were relying on odorants as the cue in the discrimination task.
source: The performance of both groups dropped to chance level in the test session (control: p=0.7241, ablation: p=0.6925, t test with chance level (0.5); Figure 2E, '50:50'), indicating that they were indeed relying on odorants as the cue.
evidence: Supported by test session data in Figure 2E where performance dropped to chance when all odorants were replaced with the same mixture.

claim: The deficits of ablation animals in the difficult 8-odorant discrimination were due to the requirement of fine discrimination and not due to the complexity of 8 different mixtures.
source: Therefore, the deficits of ablation animals in the difficult 8-odorant discrimination were due to the requirement of fine discrimination and not due to the complexity of 8 different mixtures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with the easy 8-odorant discrimination task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice without young ABNs are impaired in the difficult discrimination task requiring fine odorant discrimination.
source: In conclusion, mice without young ABNs are impaired in the difficult discrimination task requiring fine odorant discrimination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: The DG suppression mice showed comparable performance to the control group in both easy and difficult discrimination tasks.
source: During the same easy and difficult discrimination tasks described in Figure 2, the DG suppression mice showed comparable performance to the control group in both easy and difficult discrimination tasks (control vs. DG suppression; easy discrimination: number of sessions to reach expertise, p=0.8407, Wilcoxon rank sum test; difficult discrimination: p(group)=0.2663, p(session)<0.0001, 2-way ANOVA; mean ±S.E.M.; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3A,B showing no significant differences.

claim: DG postnatally-born neurons that include ABNs are not essential for fine olfactory discrimination.
source: These results indicate that DG postnatally-born neurons that include ABNs are not essential for fine olfactory discrimination and the behavioral impairment in Gfap-tk+ ablation group was primarily caused by the absence of ABNs in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DG suppression behavioral data.

claim: The behavioral impairment in Gfap-tk+ ablation group was primarily caused by the absence of ABNs in the olfactory bulb.
source: These results indicate that DG postnatally-born neurons that include ABNs are not essential for fine olfactory discrimination and the behavioral impairment in Gfap-tk+ ablation group was primarily caused by the absence of ABNs in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing Gfap-tk ablation with DG-specific suppression.

claim: After ~2 months of VGCC treatment, Gfap-tk+ ablation group have a 10.02% reduction in GCL cell density compared to Gfap-tk- controls.
source: This indicated a 10.02% reduction of total cell numbers through ABN ablation by the end of the behavioral tasks (control: n = 3, ablation: n = 4; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by DAPI quantification data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Random ablation eliminated a 19.66% reduction in GCL cell density compared with un-injected animals.
source: Post hoc DAPI staining and quantification ~1 month after injections revealed a 19.66% reduction in GCL cell density compared with un-injected animals (injected (n = 11) vs. un-injected control (n = 7): p<0.0001, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 3E,F), with no significant change in the width of GCL (injected vs. un-injected control: p=0.9499, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by DAPI quantification data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Random ablation did not affect subsequent adult neurogenesis.
source: Importantly, we found no change in Doublecortin immunostaining, indicating that our random ablation did not affect subsequent adult neurogenesis (injected (n = 7) vs. uninjected (n = 7) control, p=0.9015, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 3H,I).
evidence: Supported by Doublecortin immunostaining data in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Random ablation animals exhibited normal performance in the easy discrimination task.
source: Random ablation animals exhibited normal performance in the easy discrimination task (control vs. random ablation, number of sessions to reach expertise, p=0.4430, Wilcoxon rank sum test; mean ±S.E.M., Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3J.

claim: The random ablation group initially showed slower learning than the control group in the difficult discrimination task, but eventually reached performance level statistically indistinguishable from controls and significantly better than ABN ablation animals.
source: In the difficult discrimination task, the random ablation group initially showed slower learning than the control group, but they eventually reached the performance level that was statistically indistinguishable from the controls and significantly better than ABN ablation animals (Sessions 1–10: random ablation (n = 11) vs. control (n = 22), p=0.0034, random ablation vs. ABN ablation, p<0.0001; Sessions 1–5: random ablation vs. control, p=0.0039, random ablation vs. ABN ablation, p=0.4405; Sessions 6–10: random ablation vs. control, p=0.2028, random ablation vs. ABN ablation, p<0.0001; 2-way ANOVA; mean ±S.E.M.; Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3K with detailed statistical comparisons.

claim: Young ABNs have a privileged role in mediating fine olfactory discrimination.
source: Together with the observation that the random ablation eliminated more cells than in ABN ablation, these results support the notion that young ABNs have a privileged role in mediating fine olfactory discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing ABN ablation with random ablation results.

claim: Decoder accuracy was significantly better than chance in both control and ablation groups.
source: We found that decoder accuracy was significantly better than chance (0.125) in both control and ablation groups (control: p<0.001, ablation: p<0.001, Student's t-test; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by decoder analysis data in Figure 4E.

claim: The decoder accuracy was higher in control animals than in ablation animals.
source: However, the decoder accuracy was higher in control animals than in ablation animals (control vs. ablation, p(group)<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by decoder analysis data in Figure 4E showing significant difference.

claim: MC responses to different mixtures are more ambiguous in ablation animals than in control.
source: These results indicate that MC responses to different mixtures are more ambiguous in ablation animals than in control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoder accuracy results.

claim: Within each of the control and ablation groups, there was a positive correlation between pairwise decoder accuracy and the contrast between the mixtures.
source: We found that within each of the control and ablation groups, there was a positive correlation between pairwise decoder accuracy and the contrast between the mixtures (control: r = 0.1862, p<0.01, ablation: r = 0.3029, p<0.0001, Pearson correlation; Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by pairwise decoder analysis data in Figure 4G.

claim: The difference in decoder performance between control and ablation was more prominent in mixture pairs with smaller contrasts.
source: Although the decoder performance of the control group was generally better than the ablation group, the difference was more prominent in mixture pairs with smaller contrasts (≤3) (control vs. ablation, pairs with contrasts ≤3: p(group)<0.001, pairs with contrasts >3: p(group)=0.2530, two-way ANOVA; Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by pairwise decoder analysis data in Figure 4G showing contrast-dependent differences.

claim: ABN ablation causes the separation of MC population responses to similar odorants to be less robust.
source: These results suggest that ABN ablation causes the separation of MC population responses to similar odorants to be less robust, possibly underlying the behavioral deficits in fine discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoder analysis results.

claim: The decoder accuracy of individual animals positively correlated with their behavioral performance.
source: Consistent with this notion, the decoder accuracy of individual animals positively correlated with their behavioral performance (p<0.05, Pearson correlation; Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data in Figure 4H.

claim: The decoder performance was not affected by whether the two odorants were associated with the same or different lick sides.
source: However, the decoder performance was not affected by whether the two odorants were associated with the same or different lick sides (control: p=0.4727, ablation: p=1.0000, same vs. different associations in the bin 'contrast = 2–3', Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by decoder analysis data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fraction of MCs responsive to at least one mixture was consistently lower in ablation animals compared to control.
source: We found that the fraction of MCs responsive to at least one mixture and the fraction of responsive MC-odorant pairs were both consistently lower in ablation animals compared to control (control vs. ablation, fraction of cells: p<0.001, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.01, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by response fraction data in Figure 5A.

claim: The fraction of responsive MC-odorant pairs was consistently lower in ablation animals compared to control.
source: We found that the fraction of MCs responsive to at least one mixture and the fraction of responsive MC-odorant pairs were both consistently lower in ablation animals compared to control (control vs. ablation, fraction of cells: p<0.001, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.01, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by response fraction data in Figure 5A.

claim: The excitatory response fraction was not significantly affected by ABN ablation.
source: This analysis showed that the excitatory response fraction was not significantly affected by ABN ablation (control vs. ablation, fraction of cells: p=0.0813, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p=0.6039, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by excitatory response data in Figure 5B showing no significant difference.

claim: The decreased responses in ablation animals were primarily due to decreases in suppressive responses.
source: Instead, the decreased responses in ablation animals were primarily due to decreases in suppressive responses (control vs. ablation, fraction of cells: p<0.0001, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5C), suggesting that the net effect of ABNs on MC ensembles is inhibitory.
evidence: Supported by suppressive response data in Figure 5C showing significant differences.

claim: The net effect of ABNs on MC ensembles is inhibitory.
source: Instead, the decreased responses in ablation animals were primarily due to decreases in suppressive responses (control vs. ablation, fraction of cells: p<0.0001, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5C), suggesting that the net effect of ABNs on MC ensembles is inhibitory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that suppressive responses are reduced in ablation animals.

claim: The fraction of total responses positively correlates with decoder accuracy.
source: We found that the fraction of total (excitatory and suppressive) responses positively correlates with decoder accuracy (fraction of cells: p<0.01, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.01, Pearson correlation) and behavioral performance (cells: p<0.01; cell-odorant pairs: p<0.05; Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The fraction of total responses positively correlates with behavioral performance.
source: We found that the fraction of total (excitatory and suppressive) responses positively correlates with decoder accuracy (fraction of cells: p<0.01, fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p<0.01, Pearson correlation) and behavioral performance (cells: p<0.01; cell-odorant pairs: p<0.05; Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: When only excitatory responses were included, the relationship with decoder accuracy was not significant.
source: When we only included excitatory responses, however, this relationship was not significant (decoder accuracy, cells: p=0.2089, cell-odorant pairs: p=0.1272; performance, cells: p<0.05, cell-odorant pairs: p=0.1459; Figure 6C left and Figure 6D left).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The fraction of suppressive responses significantly correlated with both decoder accuracy and behavioral performance.
source: Instead, the fraction of suppressive responses significantly correlated with both decoder accuracy and behavioral performance (decoder accuracy, cells: p<0.01, cell-odorant pairs: p<0.01; performance, cells: p<0.05, cell-odorant pairs: p<0.05; Figure 6C right and Figure 6D right).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Young ABNs are essential for high levels of suppressive responses of MCs, which significantly contribute to odorant discriminability by MC population responses.
source: Together these results suggest that young ABNs are essential for high levels of suppressive responses of MCs, which significantly contribute to odorant discriminability by MC population responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses showing the importance of suppressive responses.

claim: In the passive condition, the fractions of MCs showing excitatory and suppressive responses were no longer statistically distinguishable between ablation and control animals.
source: Strikingly, in this passive condition, the fractions of MCs showing excitatory and suppressive responses were no longer statistically distinguishable between ablation and control animals (control passive vs. ablation passive, fraction of cells: total, p=0.6162; excitatory, p=0.7625, suppressive, p=0.2620; fraction of cell-odorant pairs: total, p=0.2043; excitatory, p=0.8691, suppressive, p=0.0625, two-way ANOVA; Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by passive exposure data in Figure 7A-C showing no significant differences.

claim: MC responses, mainly suppressive responses, are increased in a task engagement-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that MC responses, mainly suppressive responses, are increased in a task engagement-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing task and passive conditions.

claim: The interaction term for genotype and condition was statistically significant for suppressive responses.
source: The interaction term for the genotype (control vs. ablation) and the condition (task vs. passive) was statistically significant for suppressive (fraction of cells: p=0.0101; fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p=0.0239), but not excitatory (fraction of cells: p=0.1162; fraction of cell-odorant pairs: p=0.7509) responses.
evidence: Supported by linear regression model analysis.

claim: The effect of task engagement on suppressive responses is significantly larger in control animals than in ablation animals.
source: This result indicates that the effect of task engagement on suppressive, but not excitatory, responses is significantly larger in control animals than in ablation animals, supporting a role for young ABNs in enhancing suppressive responses in a task engagement-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the linear regression model analysis.

claim: Young ABNs enhance suppressive responses in a task engagement-dependent manner.
source: This result indicates that the effect of task engagement on suppressive, but not excitatory, responses is significantly larger in control animals than in ablation animals, supporting a role for young ABNs in enhancing suppressive responses in a task engagement-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of task and passive conditions.

claim: Task engagement increases the dynamic range of MC responses through top-down modulation from higher brain areas, which acts at least partially through young ABNs.
source: Taken together, we propose a model that task engagement increases the dynamic range of MC responses through top-down modulation from higher brain areas, which acts at least partially through young ABNs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Inactivation of piriform cortex enhances excitatory MC responses.
source: Consistent with this notion, inactivation of piriform cortex, a main source of feedback projections to the olfactory bulb, enhances excitatory MC responses (Otazu et al., 2015), supporting the inhibitory role of cortical feedback.
evidence: Supported by citation to Otazu et al., 2015.

claim: Experience and learning profoundly shape the representations of odorant stimuli by olfactory bulb principal neurons.
source: These dynamics of ABNs may underlie the observations that experience and learning profoundly shape the representations of odorant stimuli by olfactory bulb principal neurons (Chu et al., 2016, 2017; Doucette and Restrepo, 2008; Gschwend et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2012; Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing experience-dependent plasticity.

claim: The olfactory bulb functions as a dynamic, adaptive filter for incoming odorant information depending on behavioral demands.
source: Thus, the olfactory bulb functions as a dynamic, adaptive filter for incoming odorant information depending on behavioral demands, and adult neurogenesis is essential for this adaptive role of the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Adult neurogenesis is essential for the adaptive role of the olfactory bulb.
source: Thus, the olfactory bulb functions as a dynamic, adaptive filter for incoming odorant information depending on behavioral demands, and adult neurogenesis is essential for this adaptive role of the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Bidirectionality of MC responses effectively increases the dynamic range of MC responses.
source: The bidirectionality of responses effectively increases the dynamic range of MC responses and would contribute to an enhanced separation of representations of similar odors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of both excitatory and suppressive responses.

claim: A constant arrival and activity-dependent survival of ABNs are sufficient to separate MC representations of very similar odorants in an experience-dependent manner.
source: Consistently, a modeling study simulated the effect of adult neurogenesis on the olfactory bulb circuitry with excitatory sensory inputs, local GC inhibition and MC outputs and predicted that a constant arrival and activity-dependent survival of ABNs are sufficient to separate MC representations of very similar odorants in an experience-dependent manner (Cecchi et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cecchi et al., 2001.

claim: MC suppressive responses became more prominent during task engagement as opposed to passive exposure.
source: This is consistent with a previous report stating that suppressive responses in MCs became more prominent during task engagement as opposed to passive exposure (Fuentes et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuentes et al., 2008.

claim: Broad GC inactivation has only mild effects on MC responses under anesthesia and passive wakefulness.
source: The sensitivity to task engagement may explain the findings from a previous study that broad GC inactivation has only mild effects on MC responses under anesthesia and passive wakefulness (Fukunaga et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fukunaga et al., 2014.

claim: Synaptic inputs onto developing ABNs within different dendritic compartments formed in a sequential manner.
source: Thus, the state-dependence of the functional role of ABNs can be better appreciated considering previously reported phenomena that synaptic inputs onto developing ABNs within different dendritic compartments formed in a sequential manner (Kelsch et al., 2008), with the formation of centrifugal inputs preceding local dendrodendritic inputs (Whitman and Greer, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kelsch et al., 2008; Whitman and Greer, 2007.

claim: The formation of centrifugal inputs precedes local dendrodendritic inputs in developing ABNs.
source: Thus, the state-dependence of the functional role of ABNs can be better appreciated considering previously reported phenomena that synaptic inputs onto developing ABNs within different dendritic compartments formed in a sequential manner (Kelsch et al., 2008), with the formation of centrifugal inputs preceding local dendrodendritic inputs (Whitman and Greer, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitman and Greer, 2007.

claim: The survival rate of ABNs is sensitive to sensory experiences.
source: It has been shown that the survival rate of ABNs is sensitive to sensory experiences, which then are reflected by neuronal activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of adult neurogenesis.

claim: ABNs that are strongly activated by centrifugal inputs may have a higher chance to survive.
source: Therefore, we postulate that ABNs that are strongly activated by centrifugal inputs may have a higher chance to survive, which can explain the state-dependent requirement of ABNs for MC suppressive responses that we have observed.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the state-dependent effects.

claim: Intracellular recordings from excitatory neurons in the primary visual cortex revealed that inhibitory inputs are more prevalent in the awake state than in anesthesia.
source: Intracellular recordings from excitatory neurons in the primary visual cortex revealed that inhibitory inputs are more prevalent in the awake state than in anesthesia (Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haider et al., 2013.

claim: In the primary auditory cortex, task engagement suppresses sound-evoked responses and sharpens the tuning of excitatory neurons.
source: In the primary auditory cortex, task engagement suppresses sound-evoked responses and sharpens the tuning of excitatory neurons (Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; Otazu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; Otazu et al., 2009.

claim: The effect of task engagement on excitatory neuron tuning in auditory cortex is mediated by subtype-specific modulation of local inhibitory neurons.
source: This effect is mediated by subtype-specific modulation of local inhibitory neurons (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuchibhotla et al., 2017.

claim: Anesthesia suppresses local inhibitory neurons in the olfactory bulb.
source: In the olfactory bulb, anesthesia suppresses local inhibitory neurons (Kato et al., 2012; Wachowiak et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kato et al., 2012; Wachowiak et al., 2013.

claim: State-dependent engagement of inhibitory circuits and suppression of excitatory responses may be a common principle conserved across brain areas.
source: Together with the current study, these results suggest that state-dependent engagement of inhibitory circuits and suppression of excitatory responses may be a common principle conserved across brain areas.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings across different brain areas.

claim: In passive exposure, excitatory responses were also reduced compared to the task condition, although this effect was insensitive to ABN ablation.
source: We also note that task engagement does not only affect suppressive responses of MCs. In passive exposure, excitatory responses were also reduced compared to the task condition, although this effect was insensitive to ABN ablation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are additional, ABN-independent mechanisms modulating MC responses in a state-dependent manner.
source: Therefore, it appears that there are additional, ABN-independent mechanisms modulating MC responses in a state-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that excitatory responses are also modulated by task engagement independently of ABNs.

claim: Various feedback systems can modulate MC activity and olfactory behavior.
source: These probably include various feedback systems, which can modulate MC activity and olfactory behavior (Castillo et al., 1999; Chaudhury et al., 2009; Escanilla et al., 2010; Kapoor et al., 2016; Linster et al., 2001; Ma and Luo, 2012; Nunez-Parra et al., 2013; Rothermel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on feedback modulation.

claim: Some of the functions of feedback systems are independent of ABNs.
source: It is likely that some of the functions of these systems are independent of ABNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of ABN-independent modulation.
